quote: it seems unlikely that bond prices will remain the same
content: The finance result is the parable’s premise, not a refutation of it. If only the unexpected component of an announcement moves yields, then the pundit genuinely does not know which way the surprise will fall, his probability mass across the three outcomes is close to even, and the essay’s prescription — allocate preparation in proportion to probability — tells him to prepare all three roughly equally. That is the parable’s punchline, arrived at correctly. The target is not uniform allocation but unallocated anticipation: the pundit who has no distribution at all and discovers on Monday that he has nothing prepared.

quote: pairs of numbers, right and left numbers, which you’d call DS for Dexter-Sinister
content: Dempster–Shafer belief functions are representable as sets of probability measures, and every credal set that is used to choose an action must eventually be collapsed to a decision rule; where that rule is not expectation-maximization over a single measure, the agent is exposed to sequences of acceptable bets that lose for sure. Halpern’s counterexample to Cox concerns technical regularity conditions on the domain, and later axiomatizations repair them without changing the conclusion (Van Horn 2003). The essay’s target is not the formalism but its rhetorical use — the second number reserved so that no forecast is ever wrong — which is a use no imprecise-probability theorist endorses either.

quote: your utility function is logarithmic in time spent preparing the excuse
content: The moral of the parable is about probability; the excuse-preparation is the vehicle. Anticipation is conserved whatever your utility function, because probability sums to one, and that is the claim the essay is illustrating — you cannot expect a fire drill and also expect a chemistry lecture without taking the expectation from somewhere. The logarithmic parenthesis is there to make the time-allocation map cleanly onto the probability so a reader can see the conservation, and the essay flags it as an assumption in the same sentence. That different utilities give different allocations is true and is a fact about the vehicle.

quote: If only there were an art of focusing your uncertainty
content: Every component the annotation lists as the real source of the gains — calibration training, scoring against outcomes, aggregation — presupposes that forecasters have converted vague anticipation into numbers, which is what the essay asks for and what the untrained refuse to do. You cannot score, aggregate, or train a forecast that was never stated. Overconfidence in the untrained is a reason to add feedback, not a reason to go back to "something might happen": the tournament’s own worst performers were the ones whose judgments could not be scored at all, which is why the extremizing and aggregation machinery had something to work on in the first place (Mellers et al. 2014).
